chapter_summary:
Estimation in Agile is fundamentally different from traditional project management. Instead of providing precise, upfront time-based estimates (e.g., "this will take 40 hours"), Agile teams typically focus on **relative sizing**. This means comparing the size of one work item to another, rather than trying to predict exact durations. Why this shift? Because human beings are notoriously bad at estimating complex, creative work in absolute time, especially when there's uncertainty involved. Relative sizing, on the other hand, leverages our natural ability to compare things. It's easier to say "Task A is twice as big as Task B" than to say "Task A will take 16 hours and Task B will take 8 hours." This approach acknowledges the inherent uncertainty in software development and promotes a more collaborative and adaptive planning mindset.

The most widely used relative sizing unit in Agile is **Story Points**. A Story Point is an abstract measure of effort, complexity, and uncertainty. It's not directly tied to hours or days. When a team estimates a user story with, say, 5 story points, they are collectively agreeing that this story represents a certain amount of work relative to other stories they've estimated. For example, if a team agrees that a simple login feature is 3 story points, then a more complex feature like "integrate with a third-party payment gateway" might be 13 story points, indicating it's significantly more effort, complex, and potentially uncertain. The key is consistency within the team: once a team establishes a baseline for what a "1-point" or "3-point" story feels like, they can then relatively size all other stories. Common mistakes include trying to convert story points directly into hours or using them to compare productivity between different teams, which undermines their purpose. Story points are team-specific and are best used for forecasting within that team.

One of the most popular and effective techniques for collaborative estimation using Story Points is **Planning Poker**. This technique brings the entire development team together with the Product Owner to estimate user stories. Each team member is given a deck of cards with numbers from the Fibonacci sequence (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, etc.). The Product Owner reads a user story and clarifies any questions. Then, each team member privately selects a card representing their estimate for the story's size. On a count of three, all cards are revealed simultaneously. If estimates are close, the team quickly reaches a consensus. If there's a significant divergence (e.g., some estimate 3, others 13), the team members with the highest and lowest estimates explain their reasoning. This discussion uncovers hidden assumptions, risks, or misunderstandings, leading to a more informed and accurate collective estimate. The process repeats until a consensus is reached, or the team agrees on an estimate. Planning Poker promotes active participation, shared understanding, and prevents "anchoring" bias where early estimates influence others.

Beyond Story Points and Planning Poker, other useful relative estimation techniques exist. **T-shirt Sizing** (XS, S, M, L, XL) is often used for estimating larger items like epics or features, especially early in the product lifecycle when details are scarce. It's a quick way to get a high-level understanding of scope before diving into detailed story point estimation. **Affinity Estimation** is another visual and collaborative technique where teams group similar-sized stories together before assigning numerical values. Stories are written on cards, and team members silently place them into "buckets" representing different sizes (e.g., Small, Medium, Large). Once grouped, numerical story points are assigned to each bucket. This can be particularly effective for large backlogs or when a team is new to estimation.

A significant pitfall in Agile estimation is the temptation to use estimates as a performance metric for individuals. Story points are for forecasting team capacity and planning, not for judging how "fast" an individual developer is. Misusing estimates can lead to "gaming" the system, where developers inflate estimates to appear productive or rush through work, compromising quality. Another common mistake is neglecting to re-estimate stories that have been in the backlog for a long time or whose context has changed. As the team learns more, estimates should be refined. Remember, estimates are not commitments; they are informed guesses that help the team plan and adapt. The goal is "just enough" estimation to make informed decisions, not perfect prediction. By embracing relative sizing and collaborative techniques, Agile teams can foster a culture of transparency, shared understanding, and continuous improvement in their planning efforts.

screens.title: Agile Estimation Techniques
screens.subtitle: Relative sizing, Story Points, Planning Poker, and practical alternatives

narration.text: In this session we will learn how Agile teams estimate work using relative measures rather than precise hours. You will discover why relative sizing reduces false precision, how Story Points capture effort, complexity and uncertainty, and how collaborative techniques such as Planning Poker produce shared understanding. We will also explore quick, practical alternatives like T-shirt Sizing and Affinity Estimation for early planning. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes teams make, like converting story points into hours or using estimates as individual performance metrics. Think of estimation as a team forecasting tool, not a guarantee. For example, you will see how a simple login story can act as a baseline and how the Fibonacci sequence on Planning Poker cards reflects increasing uncertainty for larger items. By the end of these screens you will know at least three techniques to estimate and a checklist of what to avoid. Ask yourself as we go: how can your team use relative comparison to reduce rework and hidden assumptions during planning?

keyIdea.title: Why relative sizing?
keyIdea.text: Relative sizing uses comparison to reduce erroneous precision and to encourage team discussion, making planning resilient to uncertainty.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Agile Estimation Techniques
Agile Estimation Techniques
Learn how teams estimate by comparison, not by exact hours, and use collaborative rituals to surface assumptions.

Estimation in Agile focuses on relative sizing to cope with uncertainty. Story Points encode effort, complexity, and risk rather than calendar time. Planning Poker is a team ritual that turns estimation into a consensus-building conversation.

Why it matters: relative estimates reduce false precision and build shared understanding, making planning adaptive and more accurate over time.

That means you will be able to explain the limits of rigid time estimates and why comparison reduces false precision. Second, you will learn to use Story Points to capture effort, complexity and uncertainty. You will practice picking a baseline story and using it consistently so your team’s estimates are coherent. Third, you will master Planning Poker: you will know how the reveal-and-discuss cycle works, how to handle divergent estimates constructively, and how that process surfaces hidden assumptions. screens.title: Relative Sizing Explained
screens.subtitle: Why compare items instead of estimating hours

narration.text: Relative sizing is the practice of estimating work by comparison rather than by trying to predict an exact duration. That means instead of saying a story will take sixteen hours you place it against a baseline story and judge whether it is smaller, similar, or larger. This approach matters because humans are far better at comparing two items than forecasting an absolute number under uncertainty. For example, you can reliably say that a simple form field is smaller than a payment gateway integration, even if you cannot predict how many hours either will take. Relative sizing reduces the illusion of precision and helps teams communicate uncertainty explicitly. A common misconception is that relative sizes remove the need to track time. They do not: velocity and throughput still use actual delivery data for forecasting, but those forecasts start from relative estimates that are easier to produce and update. In practice, teams set a baseline — a story the team agrees is a one-point item — and then size other stories relative to that anchor. This makes estimates team-specific and consistent. The key takeaway: relative sizing trades false accuracy for shared understanding and better conversations about risk and complexity.

keyIdea.title: Compare, don't predict
keyIdea.text: Relative sizing leverages human comparative judgment to reduce false precision and surface uncertainty.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Relative Sizing Explained
What is relative sizing?
An approach that compares stories to each other instead of estimating fixed hours.
  • • Relative sizing focuses on the relationship between items: smaller, equal, or larger.
  • • Teams pick a baseline story to anchor the scale, typically a trivial item labeled 1 point.
  • • This method acknowledges uncertainty and avoids a false sense of exactness that hours imply.
Analogy
Think of sizing as comparing apples: you say this apple is twice as big as that one rather than measuring grams precisely.
Key Takeaway

Relative comparison reduces false precision and creates shared reference points for consistent team estimates.

Baseline Example
Baseline: "Add a new field to a form without validation" = 1 point.
Story A
Login with email and password
Relative size: larger than baseline; includes security and session management.
Story B
Export users to CSV
Relative size: larger than baseline; consider data volume and performance.
Common Misconception
Teams sometimes convert points to hours. That undermines the purpose: points are team-specific markers of relative effort, not a universal time unit.
Instead, use completed story points over several sprints to build a velocity-based forecast. The conversion emerges empirically from your team’s delivery history, not by decree.
Try this
Pick a 1-point baseline before your next planning session and size three backlog items relative to it to test consistency.

screens.title: Story Points: What they measure
screens.subtitle: Effort, complexity, and uncertainty — not hours

narration.text: Story Points are an abstract unit for expressing a story’s relative effort, complexity, and uncertainty. They are intentionally detached from hours, so teams avoid the trap of promising exact delivery times. When you assign a story five points you are saying that, relative to your agreed baseline, this story represents significantly more work and risk. Points typically grow non-linearly because bigger items introduce more unknowns, which is why the Fibonacci sequence is often used: the gaps increase as size grows. A useful exercise is to choose a concrete one-point example as your team’s anchor. That baseline should be trivial and repeatable so you can calibrate other estimates against it. A common misuse is converting points to hours per team member or ranking teams by points delivered; this damages trust and incentivizes gaming. Instead, treat points as internal forecasting units and derive velocity from historical completion rates. For a concrete example, imagine a login story is three points and a payment integration is thirteen points — the thirteen-point item likely needs more investigation, spikes, or risk mitigation. The practical goal is to produce consistent, comparable sizing that improves planning over time.

keyIdea.title: Points capture more than time
keyIdea.text: Story Points encode effort, hidden complexity, and uncertainty; they are a team’s internal forecasting currency, not a clock.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Story Points: What they measure
What a Story Point represents
An aggregate of effort, complexity and uncertainty, relative to the team baseline.

• Effort: how much work needs to be done, including coding, testing, and review.

• Complexity: architectural or domain difficulty, number of moving parts, and integration needs.

• Uncertainty: unknowns that could reveal new work during implementation.

Example
Login feature = 3 points, Payment integration = 13 points. The larger number signals more unknowns and likely need for spikes or architecture discussion.
Key Takeaway

Use story points to surface risk and complexity, then refine with conversation and historical velocity.

Why Fibonacci?
Larger items carry more uncertainty, so gaps increase. The Fibonacci-like scale reflects that non-linearity and encourages splitting big items.
Pitfall to avoid
Do not use story points for individual performance measurement. Points are team-specific and intended for team forecasting, not ranking or pay decisions.
Pro tip
If a story seems too large, split it. Large point values usually hide multiple concerns and increase uncertainty.

narration.text: Planning Poker is a simple ritual that turns estimation into a structured team conversation. First, the Product Owner presents a user story and answers clarifying questions. Second, each team member privately selects a card from a Fibonacci deck representing their estimate. Third, on a simultaneous reveal the team exposes differences. Fourth, those with the highest and lowest estimates explain their reasoning so the group uncovers assumptions, risks, or missing details. Fifth, the team re-estimates until they reach consensus or a workable compromise. This process is powerful because it prevents early anchoring — no one sees others’ numbers before revealing their own — and because it makes divergent thinking explicit. A common misconception is that Planning Poker wastes time; in reality the short discussion often saves time later by catching misaligned assumptions up front. For a concrete example, imagine five team members reveal 3, 5, 5, 13 and 21 for an upload story. You invite the 21 and 3 to explain. Perhaps 21 reflects concern about large image processing while 3 assumes a pre-built library. That conversation clarifies scope and leads to a shared estimate or a path to reduce risk. The outcome is a better-informed estimate and a documented assumption set.

keyIdea.title: Reveal to uncover assumptions
keyIdea.text: Simultaneous reveals and short discussions make disagreements productive and improve estimate quality.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Planning Poker — Step by step
Planning Poker Process
A five-step reveal-and-discuss technique to reach a shared estimate.
1
Discuss the story
Product Owner reads the story and answers clarifying questions so everyone understands scope.
2
Private estimate
Each team member picks a Fibonacci card privately to avoid anchoring.
3
Reveal simultaneously
All cards are shown at once so the group sees the full spread of opinions.
4
Discuss divergences
Highest and lowest estimators explain assumptions and risks to reveal hidden context.
5
Re-estimate to consensus
Repeat until the team agrees or selects a pragmatic compromise after clarifying actions.
Key Takeaway

Planning Poker avoids anchoring and makes assumptions visible, producing better shared estimates.

Example reveal
Cards shown: 3, 5, 5, 13, 21. Ask the 21 and 3 to explain — maybe 21 expects complex processing while 3 assumes a library handles most work.
Misconception
Planning Poker is not a popularity contest. It is a structured conversation: the goal is shared understanding, not forcing identical reasoning.
Check your understanding
If estimates vary widely, what specific questions will you ask to discover the biggest hidden assumption?

screens.title: Planning Poker Simulation — Stories A, B, C
screens.subtitle: Practice estimating three user stories with thoughtful reflection

narration.text: Now we’ll practice Planning Poker with three concrete user stories from the chapter. Use the previously set baseline: a one-point story is a trivial form field change. Story A asks for email-and-password login. Consider authentication logic, hashing, and session management. Some team members may estimate higher because of security or edge cases. Story B requires exporting all users to CSV. Think about database queries, pagination, and large-data performance — these risks drive larger estimates. Story C is email notifications on order status changes. If you already have an email provider integration, the complexity may be modest; otherwise it includes templating and triggers. For each story privately pick a Fibonacci value and then reveal. When estimates diverge, invite the highest and lowest estimators to explain their context: are they assuming existing libraries, or are they considering scale and error handling? Reflect on reasons for variance and whether acceptance criteria need clarification or a spike. This simulation demonstrates how Planning Poker surfaces assumptions quickly and leads to either clearer requirements or a plan to reduce risk. End the round by recording the agreed estimate and any follow-up actions such as a spike or refinement of acceptance criteria.

keyIdea.title: Simulate to surface assumptions
keyIdea.text: Run rapid poker rounds on sample stories, document divergent reasoning, and capture follow-up actions to reduce risk.

screens.title: T-shirt Sizing
screens.subtitle: Quick, high-level estimation for epics and early discovery

narration.text: T-shirt Sizing is a coarse estimation technique that uses sizes like XS, S, M, L and XL to express relative scope. It is especially useful early in the product lifecycle when stories are still epics or when details are scarce. Instead of forcing numerical story points for items with many unknowns, T-shirt Sizing gives the team a fast shared sense of scale. For example, a small refinement might be a Small while a major multi-component feature is Large. The strength of this method is speed — teams can quickly align on priority and scope without prolonged discussion. The downside is lack of precision for sprint-level planning, so T-shirt Sizing often precedes more detailed story point estimation once the work is understood. A common misconception is to treat these sizes as story points directly; instead, map sizes to points only after the team agrees on what each size implies for their context. Use T-shirt Sizing to triage, communicate a high-level roadmap, and to decide which items need deeper analysis before a point-based estimation session. T-shirt Sizing means t-shirt sizing gives a fast, shared sense of scope for epics and early discovery without forcing precise points.. In practical terms, quick, high-level estimation for epics and early discovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use T-shirt sizes for speed
keyIdea.text: T-shirt Sizing gives a fast, shared sense of scope for epics and early discovery without forcing precise points.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › T-shirt Sizing
What is T-shirt Sizing?
A fast, high-level scale using XS through XL for large or uncertain work.

• Fast alignment on scope for epics or early backlog rounds.

• Useful to triage which items need deeper analysis and which can be deferred.

• Avoid mapping sizes to precise hours until the team refines the stories.

Example mapping
XS: trivial UI tweak. S: small feature. M: multi-step feature. L/XL: cross-cutting or multi-component work that likely needs breaking down.
Key Takeaway

T-shirt Sizing speeds high-level planning and signals which items need follow-up refinement and point estimation.

When to use it
During early roadmap conversations, backlog triage, or when epics lack sufficient detail for points.
Pitfall
Do not convert sizes directly into hours or compare sizes across teams without calibration; they are context-specific.
Try this
Run a quick T-shirt Sizing round over ten backlog items to identify which need deeper refinement.

screens.title: Affinity Estimation
screens.subtitle: Group and bucket similar stories for fast backlog sizing

narration.text: Affinity Estimation is a visual, collaborative technique for quickly grouping similar-sized stories. Team members silently place story cards into buckets that represent relative sizes, then the group assigns numerical values to each bucket. This method is highly effective when you have a large backlog or when onboarding a new team because it minimizes long debates by letting natural clustering appear. Start by picking a handful of sample stories and create empty buckets labeled Small, Medium, Large, and so on. Team members move cards into buckets based on their sense of relative effort. Once grouped, assign story points to buckets and refine outliers. A common pitfall is over-discussing every card; keep the first pass fast and then discuss only questionable placements. Affinity Estimation also helps identify patterns: if many cards cluster as Large, you may have many epics that need breaking down. The goal is speed with enough accuracy to prioritize and to identify which items should be re-estimated in more detail during sprint planning. Affinity Estimation means affinity estimation groups similar stories quickly and assigns points to buckets, making large backlogs manageable.. In practical terms, group and bucket similar stories for fast backlog sizing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cluster to scale
keyIdea.text: Affinity Estimation groups similar stories quickly and assigns points to buckets, making large backlogs manageable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Affinity Estimation
Affinity Estimation steps
A silent, visual grouping technique for bulk backlog sizing.
  1. Prepare story cards and an open board with empty buckets (Small, Medium, Large).
  2. Team silently places cards into buckets based on perceived similarity.
  3. Review placements and move obvious outliers.
  4. Assign story points to each bucket and refine ambiguous cards.
Why it works
Silence reduces anchoring. Visual grouping reveals natural clusters and speeds bulk sizing.
Key Takeaway

Affinity Estimation makes large backlog sizing fast and identifies where refinement effort should be focused.

Practical tip
Keep the first pass under ten minutes and only discuss cards that multiple people placed into different buckets.
Common mistake
Debating every card defeats the purpose. Use silence and quick passes to let natural similarity emerge before refining.
Try this
Run affinity on a 50-item backlog subset to find high-level clusters and then assign point ranges per bucket.

screens.title: Choosing the Right Technique
screens.subtitle: When to use Story Points, T-shirt Sizing, or Affinity Estimation

narration.text: Selecting the correct estimation technique depends on context. Use Story Points and Planning Poker when you need sprint-level detail and the team has enough information to compare stories reliably. This method shines for well-groomed backlogs and when you want a repeatable forecasting unit. Use T-shirt Sizing early in discovery or for epics when details are minimal; it gives a fast sense of scope without wasting time on precise points. Affinity Estimation works best for large backlogs or onboarding, where you want to group similar items quickly. A helpful mental model: if you need precision and sprint planning, lean toward story points; if you need speed and a rough roadmap, use T-shirt Sizing; if you need to process many items, pick Affinity. A common mistake is mixing methods without clear purpose — for example, running T-shirt Sizing and then immediately forcing points without re-discussion can produce inconsistent baselines. Instead, allow T-shirt or Affinity rounds to inform which items require a follow-up Planning Poker session for accurate sprint planning. The practical effect is faster grooming and clearer prioritization when the technique matches the planning need.

keyIdea.title: Match method to context
keyIdea.text: Choose story points for detailed sprint planning, T-shirt for early scope, and affinity for bulk backlog work.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Choosing the Right Technique
Compare techniques
A quick guide to when each method is most effective.
Story Points + Planning Poker
Use for sprint-level planning and consistent forecasting when stories are well understood.
T-shirt Sizing
Use during early discovery or roadmap planning to get a high-level sense of scope quickly.
Affinity Estimation
Use for large backlogs and bulk sizing; it clusters similar items fast and reduces meeting overhead.
Decision rule
If you need detail for the next sprint choose points. If you need speed for roadmap planning choose T-shirt. For many items choose Affinity.
Common error
Avoid switching methods mid-stream without recalibrating your baseline; different approaches create different reference frames.
Try this
Run a T-shirt pass to triage, then pick ten mid-priority items for Planning Poker to validate sprint forecasts.

screens.title: Common Estimation Mistakes
screens.subtitle: What to avoid and how to correct it

narration.text: Several common mistakes undermine the value of Agile estimation. First, using story points as a performance metric for individuals encourages gaming and undermines trust. Points are intended for team forecasting, not measuring personal speed. Second, converting story points directly into hours and promising fixed delivery dates defeats the point of relative sizing; it creates false precision and brittle commitments. Third, failing to re-estimate stale backlog items means estimates become outdated as context changes; re-evaluate items when requirements shift. Fourth, allowing anchoring bias by revealing estimates too early or by the Product Owner suggesting a number breaks the consensus process. Corrective strategies include: keep points for team forecasting only, derive velocity empirically from completed work, re-estimate periodically or at refinement, and preserve private estimates until the reveal. For example if a team used points to compare across teams, they would get misleading productivity metrics because points are calibrated per team context. The practical remedy: treat estimates as informed guesses, record assumptions, and use follow-up spikes to reduce large uncertainties when needed. Common Estimation Mistakes means use points for team forecasting, re-estimate when context shifts, and keep estimates private until reveal to reduce bias.. In practical terms, what to avoid and how to correct it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid misuse of estimates
keyIdea.text: Use points for team forecasting, re-estimate when context shifts, and keep estimates private until reveal to reduce bias.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Common Estimation Mistakes
Frequent anti-patterns
A compact checklist of mistakes and fixes.
  • Points as performance: discourage using story points to measure individuals; use throughput and quality metrics instead.
  • Points → hours: avoid imposing direct conversions; velocity should be learned from history.
  • Stale estimates: re-estimate items after significant changes or before committing to a sprint.
  • Anchoring bias: keep estimates private until the reveal to encourage independent thinking.
Correction
Record assumptions, run short spikes for risky stories, and derive velocity from delivered work rather than declared hours.
Example misuse
If management compares teams by points delivered, teams with different baselines will be unfairly ranked. Points are team-relative.
Pro tip
Document the baseline story and major assumptions after each poker session so future reviewers understand the original context of the estimate.
Key Takeaway
Keep estimates as team tools for planning, not as measures of individual speed; re-evaluate as the context evolves.

screens.title: From Estimates to Forecasts
screens.subtitle: Using velocity and conservative planning without mistaking estimates for commitments

narration.text: Estimates become useful when you use them to forecast work at the team level. Velocity is the empirical number of story points a team completes per sprint. Use past velocity to inform how much new work the team can reasonably take on, but remember that velocity itself evolves as the team changes and as work differs in type. A conservative approach is to use a rolling average of completed points rather than a single sprint peak. Also, treat estimates as informed guesses not commitments; communicate uncertainty and record follow-up actions like spikes when needed. For planning, select a subset of groomed stories whose total points align with a conservative velocity estimate, and leave buffer for interruptions. Avoid promising a fixed date solely based on points without accounting for variability. A common misconception is that accurate estimates guarantee timely delivery; they help reduction of uncertainty and decision-making but cannot eliminate all risk. Use forecasts to set expectations, not absolutes. The practical habit: update estimates during backlog refinement and re-run Planning Poker after significant requirement changes to keep forecasts aligned with reality.

keyIdea.title: Forecast, don't promise
keyIdea.text: Use rolling velocity for conservative forecasts and treat estimates as evolving inputs that inform decisions, not guarantees.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › From Estimates to Forecasts
Turning points into plans
Use velocity as an empirical guide and maintain conservative buffers.

• Compute a rolling average of completed story points across several sprints to reduce variability.

• Select backlog items whose total points fit a conservative velocity for sprint planning and leave capacity for interruptions.

• Re-estimate stories when requirements change and record spikes as follow-up actions to reduce uncertainty.

Key Takeaway

Use velocity-derived forecasts with caution: they guide decisions but do not replace ongoing refinement and transparency about risk.

Example practice
If your 3-sprint rolling average is 20 points, pick 16–18 points for the next sprint to allow for slack and unexpected work.
Misconception
Don’t expect estimates to be static. Revisit them as the team gains knowledge and as acceptance criteria evolve.
Try this
Calculate your team’s 3-sprint rolling velocity and plan the next sprint at 80–90% of that average to maintain a realistic buffer.

narration.text: Let’s summarize the three core concepts you should keep with you. First, Relative Sizing: estimate by comparison to reduce false precision. Use a consistent baseline so your team’s estimates are coherent. Second, Story Points: they capture effort, complexity and uncertainty; they are not hours and should not be used to evaluate individual performance. Third, Planning Poker: a reveal-and-discuss technique that prevents anchoring and surfaces assumptions by having private estimates followed by short discussions. Each concept supports the same goal: better planning through shared understanding, not through forced precision. Keep in mind the alternatives — T-shirt Sizing for early discovery and Affinity Estimation for bulk backlog work — and the common pitfalls such as converting points to hours or using points as a metric of individual productivity. These ideas together create a practical, human-centered approach to estimation that scales from one sprint to long-term roadmap decisions. narration.text: Before we finish, keep three practical reminders: calibrate a clear baseline story and use it consistently; run Planning Poker to make differing assumptions visible and to reach a shared estimate; and pick the right method — T-shirt Sizing or Affinity — when you need speed or bulk processing. Also remember that estimates are not commitments; treat them as evolving information and re-estimate when important context changes. A practical next step is to run a short Planning Poker simulation with your team using one baseline story and three backlog items, documenting assumptions after each reveal. This simple habit builds a stronger planning rhythm and reduces surprises in sprint execution.
